# Expectation

## Defining the Expectation of a Random Variable

A random variable is a quantity the draw decides. Its expectation says where
the distribution sits, before any sample:

$$
E[y] \;=\; \sum_{j} y_j \, p_j
$$

- $y$: the variable, here hourly earnings in euro
- $j$: which value, running over every value $y$ can take
- $y_j$: one value that $y$ can take
- $p_j$: the share of the population sitting at that value
- $E[y]$: the population average of $y$, here 11.52 euro

::: {.notes}
IDEA 1. 10-33 min. Weight each value by how common it is. That is the whole
content; the sum is not the idea.

Say on the board that for a variable taking a continuum of values the sum
becomes an integral, and that nothing on this slide changes when it does. We
will not compute an integral in this module, but they should not leave
believing an expectation is only defined for a short list of values.
:::

## Notation for the Population Mean and the Sample Mean

From here every summary comes as a pair: one population, one sample.

::: {.defn title="The Population Mean Is Fixed, the Sample Mean Is Not"}
$E[y]$ is one fixed number, a property of the distribution. $\bar y$ is the
sample average, 12.25 in our 120. Draw a different 120 and $\bar y$ is a
different number.
:::

::: {.notes}
This distinction is the one that has to survive the term. A bar means computed
from a sample; a bare letter means true of the population. A student who reads
the two as the same object cannot be taught sampling variation, which is the
whole of Lecture 1.3.

Later in the module the bar gives way to a hat on quantities that estimate a
parameter. Do not promise a week for that here; the two deck headers disagree
about whether it lands in 1.3 or 2.1, and it is not settled.
:::

## The Gap Between the Two Lines Has Its Own Distribution

Every claim this module makes is about the solid line. Every number we compute
comes from the dashed one.

::: {.takeaway title="Lectures 1.3 and 2.3 Measure the Gap"}
The 0.73 between 12.25 and 11.52 is not a mistake to be removed. That gap
changes with every sample drawn. A standard error puts a number on it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three averages of hourly earnings are now in play: our 120 people, E[y], and
all 200,000. Only the first can change.

This is also why an expectation is not "the average of a big enough dataset".
It is a feature of the process that generated the data. Our population happens
to be finite, so its own average and $E[y]$ coincide here; that is a property
of how we built it, not of expectations.
:::

# The Algebra of Expectations

## The Three Rules of Expectation Algebra

Measuring that gap means averaging combinations of variables. Three rules do
that without knowing the combination's distribution:

$$
E[c] = c \qquad\qquad E[a + b\,y] = a + b\,E[y] \qquad\qquad E[y + z] = E[y] + E[z]
$$

- $c$: a fixed number, with no distribution of its own
- $a$, $b$: a shift and a scaling, applied identically to every draw
- $z$: a second random variable, related to $y$ or not; the rule holds either way

::: {.defn title="A Constant Is the Same in Every Draw"}
An expectation averages across draws. A constant does not change from draw to draw,
so averaging it returns it unchanged. A fixed multiplier factors out of the sum. On the right-hand side only
$y$ and $z$ still carry an $E$, because only they vary.
:::

::: {.notes}
IDEA 2. 36-60 min. Say each one out loud in words, and say what it buys, before
any symbols go up.

Answer the question on the box before it is asked, because it is the one that
stops people. Why does the $E$ come off $a$ and $b$ and stay on $y$? Because an
expectation is an average over draws, and only things that change from draw to
draw have anything to average. Draw a person, draw another, draw a third: their
earnings differ, the tax rate does not.

Say plainly what a constant is NOT. It is not a number we happen to know. A
population slope is a constant and nobody knows it, and it still comes out of
an expectation, because it is one fixed number for the whole population rather
than something that varies person to person. That distinction is the reason
Lecture 2.3 can write $E[\hat{\beta}] = \beta$ at all, so plant it here.

The constant rule: a fee or a tax rate comes through the average untouched and
needs no distribution at all. The linear rule: report earnings in cents instead
of euro and the average rescales by 100, without going back to the 200,000
people. Additivity: the average of a total is the total of the averages, so an
estimator built by adding up 120 draws can be averaged one draw at a time.

HEAD OFF THE SLOPE READING OF $b$. In econometrics $b$ almost always means a
slope, so a room that has seen any regression reads this rule as being about
one, and then cannot see why it is allowed out of the expectation. It is not a
slope here. It is a unit conversion: euro to cents, gross pay to take-home,
Celsius to Fahrenheit. We choose it and apply the same number to everyone, and
nothing is being estimated. Give the cents example and move on.

Then, if the question comes - and it does - say where the two meet. The slope
of a regression, $\beta$, is also a constant, but for a different reason. It is
not one we chose; it is one number the population has, the amount the
conditional average of $y$ changes per unit of $x$. And saying it is ONE number
is exactly the straight-line assumption: a slope is a ratio of changes, so
calling it constant claims that ratio is the same everywhere along $x$. If the
CEF bends there is no single slope to take outside anything. That is the honest
version of "we wrote the generator that way" three frames on, and it is worth
holding until then rather than opening it here.

Without the three, every new combination of variables would need its own
distribution worked out from scratch. That is the work they save.

ADDITIVITY NEEDS NO INDEPENDENCE. The $z$ bullet now says so, so read it out.
Averages add whatever the joint distribution is: $y$ and $z$ may be dependent
and the third rule still holds. Wooldridge states it for any number of variables
with any constants in front of them, with no independence assumption anywhere.
Worth the extra thirty seconds, because two frames on they meet a variance rule
that does need a condition, and the contrast is the point.
:::

## Variance and Covariance Written as Expectations

Spread and co-movement are themselves averages, so the three rules reach them:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(y) \;=\; E\big[(y - E[y])^2\big] \;=\; E[y^2] - \big(E[y]\big)^2
$$

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(y, x) \;=\; E\big[(y - E[y])(x - E[x])\big] \;=\; E[yx] - E[y]\,E[x]
$$

- $x$: years of schooling
- $\operatorname{Var}(y)$: the population variance, written $\sigma_y^2$ in Lecture 1.1
- $\operatorname{Cov}(y,x)$: the population co-movement of the two
- $E[y^2]$: the average of the squares, not the square of the average

::: {.notes}
$\operatorname{Var}(y)$ is the population spread of $y$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(y,x)$
is the population co-movement of $y$ and $x$; both were defined last week on the
sample, and these are the population versions.

The right-hand forms are the ones used for calculation. Point at the second
line and say that the last term is what the next frame is about.
:::

## Why Expectations Do Not Pass Through a Product

An expectation passes through sums, constants and scalings, and not through a
product. Independent means knowing one variable tells you nothing about the
other. Last week the covariance of schooling and earnings in our 120 came out
positive, so these two are not independent.

::: {.takeaway title="The Product Rule Fails by the Covariance"}
$E[yx] = E[y]E[x] + \operatorname{Cov}(y,x)$. The two agree exactly when the
covariance is zero. Independence gives that; the equality does not need it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read it off the line above: $\operatorname{Cov}(y,x) = E[yx] - E[y]E[x]$, so the
product rule fails by exactly the covariance and holds exactly when the
covariance vanishes. It is an equivalence in both directions.

Independent variables are uncorrelated, so independence is enough. Uncorrelated
variables need not be independent, so independence is not required. Wooldridge
gives the standard counter-example: a variable with mean zero and zero third
moment has zero covariance with its own square, and a variable and its square
are about as dependent as two variables get.

Last week they measured a positive covariance between schooling and earnings in
this sample, so for these two the product rule fails in a direction they can
already sign. Do not sign it for them here: the question frame later in this
section is exactly that, and the slide gives them the covariance and the
equivalence, which is everything they need to do it themselves.
:::

## The Variance of a Sum Carries a Covariance Term

Adding two random variables does not add their variances:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(y + z) \;=\; \operatorname{Var}(y) + \operatorname{Var}(z) + 2\operatorname{Cov}(y, z)
$$

::: {.takeaway title="Zero Covariance Drops the Term"}
The covariance term drops out when $y$ and $z$ are uncorrelated. Independence is
stronger than this rule asks for.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two things to say. First, the sign: a positive covariance makes the sum more
variable than the two variances suggest, a negative one makes it less. Second,
the condition: uncorrelated is enough, and the commonest error in a first
course is to write independence here.

The same rule for a difference still adds the variances: subtracting a variable
does not subtract its spread. Worth putting on the board.

This is the rule Lecture 2.3 uses to get a standard error, so it is stated
here rather than assumed there.
:::

## Where Each Rule Is Used Later in the Module

- **Linearity:** cuts the Lecture 2.3 proof of unbiasedness to two lines from twenty.
- **The Variance of a Sum:** builds next week's standard error, and 2.3's.
- **Covariance Over Variance:** $\operatorname{Cov}(y,x)/\operatorname{Var}(x)$ is the slope Lecture 2.1 fits.

::: {.takeaway title="Each Rule Is the Sum Rearranged"}
The appendix writes the weighted sum, splits it, then takes the constants
outside.
:::

::: {.notes}
The step that does the work is the splitting, and it works because summation
splits across addition and nothing else. That is also why no step of the same
kind is available for a product, and why the covariance term survives.

Full derivation in the appendix, set as homework. Class time goes on the shape
of the proof, not on the algebra.

This is the only slide in the module where the algebra arrives before its use.
Everything else is introduced where it first bites, and it is worth telling them
that, so the ordering does not read as an accident.

The slope is written out on the third bullet. They have not been told what it
is for.
:::

# The Conditional Expectation Function

## Defining the Conditional Expectation of Earnings Given Schooling

A covariance says these two vary together. It does not say what to expect at a
given level of schooling. Split by schooling, then average inside each group:

$$
E[y \mid x]
$$

- $E[y \mid x]$: read "given"; the average of $y$ among people with that $x$

In a sample it is the mean from Lecture 1.1, taken over a chosen group:

$$
\bar{y}_{\,x = 12} \;=\; \frac{1}{n_{12}} \sum_{i \,:\, x_i = 12} y_i
$$

- $\sum_{i \,:\, x_i = 12}$: add over only the people with twelve years
- $n_{12}$: how many of our 120 have twelve years

::: {.defn title="A Function, Not a Number"}
$E[y \mid x]$ is the conditional expectation function, the CEF for short. The CEF
returns a different average at each value of $x$.
:::

::: {.notes}
IDEA 3. 63-90 min. Do the physical example before the earnings one, because it
costs thirty seconds and it makes the whole object concrete. Measure everyone's
height. Now sort them into weight bands and take the average height inside each
band. The sequence of averages you get is a CEF. Nothing else is going on: it is
a local average, where "local" means a group defined by the other variable.

Then say what the sorting buys. Someone walks in and you have to name their
hourly earnings; you are told only how long they stayed in school. The number
you would say is the average of the group they fall into, and the whole of
Lecture 2.1 is an attempt to estimate it.

One nuance worth a sentence, because it recycles Lecture 1.1's notation rule.
Splitting a sample into bins and averaging gives the SAMPLE version. The CEF
itself is the population object, a fact about all 200,000. The Roman-and-Greek
distinction from Lecture 1.1 applies here to a whole function rather than to a
single number, and the figure two frames on shows the sample version standing
in for the population one.

The second display is there to stop this looking like a new formalism. Read the
right-hand side out in words - add up the earnings of everyone with twelve years
of schooling, divide by how many of them there are - and it is the mean from
Lecture 1.1 with a condition on which rows enter the sum. No new algebra, no new
operator: the only thing the bar does is decide who is in the average. Every
year someone asks whether expectation is different from averaging, and this is
the frame that answers it, so do not skip past the display.

"Best" is a precise claim, not a compliment, and the frame two on gives the
precise version: smallest expected squared error. Promise it here rather than
leaving the word loose.

Then read it aloud as "the average of earnings among everyone in the population
with this much schooling". Feed it twelve and it returns 9.50; feed it sixteen
and it returns 14.70.

Wooldridge's own example is the same pair of variables: hourly wage given years
of education, with $E[\text{wage} \mid \text{educ}]$ traced out across education
levels. Say that, so they know this is not a device invented for this module.
:::

## The Conditional Expectation Function in This Population

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/1-2_cef-weights.png}{One hundred people drawn for this picture; each navy point is that column's average.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Counts Are the Weights"}
The blue line is the CEF written into the generator, $E[y \mid x] = 9.50 +
1.30\,(x - 12)$. Pooling all one hundred gives 10.70. Averaging the ten column
means without their counts gives 11.61, weighting two people at eighteen years
like twenty at twelve.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk it column by column. Ten levels of schooling, one hundred people spread
unevenly across them, and the navy dot in each column is the average of the pale
dots under it. Nothing else is happening. That is the whole of the conditional
expectation, done ten times.

The bar inside each box is the median and the navy dot is the mean, which is
Lecture 1.1's distinction on a real picture. Point at a skewed column
and note that the two do not coincide.

Then the second reading, which is the one worth the time. The green rule is the
average of all one hundred, 10.70. The dotted rule is the average of the ten
navy dots, 11.61. Ask why they differ before saying why: the ten columns are not
the same size, so treating them as ten equal things overweights the empty end.
The counts under the columns are the weights, and ignoring them costs ninety-one
cent here.

That is also the answer to the question that comes up every year, whether an
expectation is "just an average". It is. Pooled, every person counts once and
you need no weights at all. Reassembled from group averages, the group sizes are
the weights and dropping them changes the number.

The blue line is straight because we wrote the generator that way. Nothing in
the definition of a conditional expectation requires it, and the question frame
later in this section is exactly that point.

Say "goes with", not "raises". This is a description of the population, and
today's last section is about how easily it gets read as an effect.
:::

## The Sense in Which the Conditional Mean Is Best

No rule built on schooling beats the conditional mean on squared error:

$$
E[y \mid x] \;=\; \arg\min_{g} \; E\big[\,(y - g(x))^2\,\big]
$$

- $g(x)$: any function of $x$ used to guess $y$
- $\arg\min_{g}$: the $g$ that makes what follows as small as it goes

::: {.caveat title="Both Expected Squares Must Be Finite"}
Both $E[y^2]$ and $E[g(x)^2]$ must be finite. Without them there is no expected
squared error to compare.
:::

::: {.notes}
The comparison class is the part that matters. It is not straight lines, not
smooth functions, not simple functions: it is every function of $x$ with a
finite expected square. That is what makes "best guess" a result rather than a
preference.

Say the straight-line case out loud, because it is the one Lecture 2.1 inherits:
straight lines are in the class, and they lose to the CEF unless the CEF is
itself a straight line.

Wooldridge states the inequality twice: conditional on $x$, and unconditionally.
The unconditional form is the one written here, and it follows from the
conditional one. Say that, and leave the proof to the appendix.

The finiteness conditions are not decoration. Without them the minimisation is
not well posed, and "no rule does better" would be a claim about objects with no
expected squared error to compare.
:::

## Why the Minimum Sits at the Conditional Mean

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Expected squared error at twelve years of schooling, against the guess made.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Minimum Is the Conditional Variance"}
The curve is lowest at a guess of 9.50, at a height of $4.50^2$. That height is
the conditional variance, and no guess goes below it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three steps, and they are in the appendix: add and subtract the conditional mean
inside the square, expand, and show the cross term has expectation zero. The step
doing the work is the third.

Why the cross term has expectation zero: it is a deviation from the conditional
mean multiplied by something fixed once $x$ is known, so averaging within each
value of $x$ sends it to zero. That is Property CE.2 doing the work.

Walk the picture: candidate guesses on the horizontal axis, expected squared
error on the vertical, one convex curve, minimum at 9.50. The height of the
minimum is the conditional variance, and that height is not zero. Every other
guess sits above the floor by a squared term, which is why the curve is convex
and why the minimum is unique.
:::

<!-- FIGURE 1-2_mse: horizontal axis a candidate constant guess c running from
     about 4 to 15, vertical axis E[(y - c)^2 | x = 12], one convex curve with

## What the Fitted Line in Lecture 2.1 Approximates

Without the CEF, a fitted line is the easiest curve to draw.
@angrist2015 build the regression chapters of *Mastering Metrics* on the CEF.

::: {.takeaway title="The Line Approximates the CEF"}
Lecture 2.1 fits a line by least squares to approximate the CEF. This
population's CEF is straight; real ones need not be. The CEF exists
in the population before anyone fits anything.
:::

::: {.notes}
The fitted line is an answer to a question already posed, not a summary chosen
because it is easy to draw. That is the whole reason conditional expectation is
in Lecture 1.2 rather than in an appendix.

Mastering Metrics opens its regression theory appendix on the CEF and then puts
the regression line through a real earnings-on-schooling CEF, which bounces
around the line rather than lying on it. Worth describing out loud; it is the
picture Lecture 2.1 will earn.

## Description Versus Causation in the Conditional Mean

Describing who earns what is not the same as saying what schooling does.

::: {.caveat title="A Description, Not an Effect"}
$E[y \mid x]$ describes the population and says nothing about changing $x$.
"People with sixteen years of schooling earn 14.70 on average" is a description.
"Four more years raises earnings by 5.20" is a different claim. Nothing today
supports it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Hold this distinction. Lecture 4.2 is built entirely on it.

Mastering Metrics runs Mincer's earnings regression on the 1960 census, gets
about eleven per cent a year with experience controls, and then asks whether
more- and less-educated workers at the same experience level are equally able
and diligent. Their own answer is that such claims are hard to swallow, and the
gap between the description and the effect is the subject of the rest of that
chapter.
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

Today's number is the conditional mean of earnings at each level of schooling.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

::: {.notes}
90-95 min. Same slot every week. They answer in pairs first, then you.

The answer, once they have had a go: reading $E[y \mid x]$ as an effect is an
assumption about who stayed in school, and stayers and leavers must differ in
nothing else touching earnings. The point is not that causation is hard in the
abstract; it is that THIS number rests on something nameable that may well be
false.

This used to be printed on the slide, under the box, which answered the question
before the room was asked it. Lecture 1.1's version of this frame carries its
context above the box and nothing below, and this one now matches.

## Derivation: The Algebra of Expectations

Write each expectation as its weighted sum, split it, take the constants outside.

::: {.takeaway title="Three Rules, the Variance Form Follows"}
Three rules follow: a constant, a linear function, and a sum. The variance form
$E[y^2] - (E[y])^2$ is a consequence of them, not a fourth rule.
:::

::: {.notes}
The step that does the work throughout is splitting the sum, which is available
for addition and for nothing else. Where you cannot split, a covariance term
survives, and that surviving term is the whole of the slope formula in Lecture
2.1.

Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-3b, p.692-693, for E.1, E.2 and E.3, derived from (B.17).
     B-3e, p.695, equation (B.24), for the variance form.

     CORRECTION. This frame said "Four results" and the body slide called them
     "the four rules". B-3b gives three properties of expected values; the
     variance form is B-3e and is a consequence, not a fourth property. The
     frame now says three rules and one consequence, and the body frame is
     retitled "The Three Rules of Expectation Algebra". -->
```

## Derivation: The Conditional Mean Minimises Expected Squared Error

Add and subtract $E[y \mid x]$ inside the square, then expand. The cross term has
expectation zero.

::: {.takeaway title="The Cross Term Has Mean Zero"}
Assume $E[y^2]$ and $E[g(x)^2]$ are finite. What remains is the conditional
variance plus a squared term, zero only at $g(x) = E[y \mid x]$.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three steps. The third is the one that works: the cross term is a deviation from
the conditional mean multiplied by something fixed once $x$ is known, so
averaging within each value of $x$ sends it to zero.

That is the entire content of "best guess". Set as homework; worked solution
published with the set.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-4f, p.703, Property CE.6, with its two finiteness
     conditions, and Property CE.2 on p.702, which is what sends the cross
     term to zero. B-4g, p.704, for the conditional variance left behind.

     CORRECTION. The finiteness conditions were absent here and on the body
     frame. CE.6 is stated with them. -->
```

## Notes and Tools

- **Binning in R:** `cut()` and `tapply()`, which is the whole binned-means lab.
- **The Lecture in One Line:** `mean(y[x == 12])` against `mean(y)`.
- **This Week's Script:** the CEF explorer, and the code that draws its exhibits.
